label: text
content: ## "Progressive" multiple alignments

label: text
content: - The idea of progressive alignment is to keep aligning pairs of sequences (or of alignment profiles) following their evolutionary history backwards

label: text
content: - That is, we start by aligning the strings that are the "closest relatives" (most recent divergence), then we move backwards to the more distant history

label: text
content: The key is having the "guide-tree" telling us the order of operations in which the alignment has to be built:

label: text
content: Example: according to the evolutionary tree to the left, we ...

label: text
content: 1 Align S1 with S2 to build the alignment profile P(S1,S2)

label: text
content: 2 Align S3 with S4 to build the alignment profile P(S3,S4)

label: text
content: 3 Align P(S1,S2) with P(S3,S4) to derive the final alignment (S1,S2,S3,S4)

label: text
content: - We need a "guide tree" which represents the evolutionary history (and thus the order of operations) before proceeding with the alignments ...

label: text
content: - Note: in this progressive procedure the algorithm never actually evaluates the score associated with an alignment; it just builds the final solution step-by-step!

label: text
content: ## "Progressive" multiple alignments

label: text
content: - Idea: we build the guide tree ourselves, that is, we try to guess the evolutionary history behind the sequences

label: text
content: The tree should give us an estimate of the evolutionary history of the sequences

label: text
content: The general principle/assumption behind the tree is: "The more two strings are similar, the more recent is the evolutionary event that produced them"

label: text
content: - Thus, a good idea would be to build the tree going "back in time"

label: text
content: We start from the final sequences, and derive their common ancestors

label: text
content: We start from the leaves and move up the tree. Every time we find an internal node, we meet an evolutionary event (e.g., speciation)

label: text
content: ## Building the guide tree

label: text
content: - We start again by comparing all sequences and compute their pairwise distances

label: text
content: - We proceed in a "greedy" way: we choose the pair with minimal distance, align them and build their profile

label: text
content: - Suppose that the closest pair is S1-S2: we have the first node of the tree, and call A(S1,S2) their alignment

label: text
content: - The alignment represents their common ancestor, and it will be part of the final multiple alignment

label: text
content: Step 1: S1 and S2 are the strings at minimum distance among all pairs

label: text
content: ## Building the guide tree

label: text
content: - At the second step, we have three objects:

label: text
content: - Alignment A(S1,S2)

label: text
content: ★ This replaces S1 and S2!

label: text
content: String S3

label: text
content: String S4

label: text
content: - We choose again the closest pair among the three possibilities

label: text
content: - Distance between A(S1,S2) and S3

label: text
content: - Distance between A(S1,S2) and S4

label: text
content: - Distance between S3 and S4 [computed already for step 1!]

label: text
content: - Suppose that the best choice (minimal distance) is the third. We align S3 and S4, and add the node A(S3,4) to the tree

label: text
content: Step 2: S3 and S4 are the strings at minimum distance among all pairs. We generate a new node and the corresponding alignment A(S3,S4)

label: text
content: ## Building the guide tree

label: text
content: - At the third step, we have two objects left:

label: text
content: - Alignment A(S1,S2)

label: text
content: - Alignment A(S3,S4)

label: text
content: Only one choice. We align the two alignments, represented by their profiles

label: text
content: No matter what the initial number k of sequences is, we will always have a final merge of two alignments and/or sequences!

label: text
content: - The result is A(S1,S2,S3,S4), which is the final alignment!

label: text
content: - Note: we have built the guide tree and constructed the final multiple alignment at the same time!

label: text
content: Step 3: We align A(S1,S2) and A(S3,S4) and have reached the root of the tree

label: text
content: ## Building the guide tree

label: text
content: This approach is a greedy strategy

label: text
content: - At each step we chose the best alternative

label: text
content: From another point of view, this performs a hierarchical clustering of the strings

label: text
content: - Replace "align" with "cluster" in what we have seen so far:

label: text
content: Every time we align two strings, we put them in the same cluster

label: text
content: Every time we align a string to a profile, we add it to an existing cluster

label: text
content: Every time we align two profiles, we merge two clusters

label: text
content: - At the end, we will have one single cluster comprising all strings

content: ## Hierarchical clustering

label: text
content: ## Hierarchical clustering is one of a set of related data mining techniques

label: text
content: (Clustering of nucleo-cytoplasmic large DNA viruses based on the presence or absence of orthologous genes; from: Bajrai et al, 2016)

label: text
content: - Edge length is often depicted proportionally to the computed distance

label: text

label: text
content: ## Clustering

label: text
content: "Clustering" (not only hierarchical clustering) is a very important branch for data mining, machine learning, and statistics

label: text
content: - Clustering algorithms can be divided into many sub-branches, e.g., according to

label: text
content: - whether the number of expected clusters is known beforehand (e.g., k-means clustering)

label: text
content: - whether it is supervised or unsupervised

label: text
content: - whether it is hierarchical, centroid-based, density-based, ...

label: text
content: - Clustering can be applied to different kinds of data, mainly numerical, but also as in our example, to sequences

label: text
content: - Each item to be clustered is seen as a point in a multi-dimensional space: the only thing needed is a suitable distance measure

label: text
content: Different distance (or similarity) measures can be applied, for example

label: text
content: ★ Edit distance or alignment score (for sequences)

label: text
content: - Euclidean distance, cosine similarity or correlation coefficients (for numeric data)

label: text
content: ## For two sequences, we define a distance measure by "scaling" the similarity score obtained from alignment

label: text
content: - But what is the "distance" between a sequence and an alignment or between two alignments?

label: text
content: ## Building the guide tree

label: text
content: At each step, we decide to "join" the two closest objects:

label: text
content: Two strings

label: text
content: - One strings and an alignment (a cluster)

label: text
content: - Two alignments (two clusters)

label: text
content: For measuring the distance between two strings, we just take the distance given by their alignment

label: text
content: - But how do we measure the distance between one string and an alignment or between two alignments?

label: text
content: - This is a problem well studied in clustering, that is:

label: text
content: - Define a distance measure between a point and a cluster

label: text
content: - Define a distance measure between two clusters

label: text
content: How do we compute the distances between S3 and A(S1,S2) and between S4 and A(S1,S2) to decide the next step?

label: text
content: ## Measuring distances

label: text
content: For the distance between a string and an alignment (cluster of strings), we have these main choices:

label: text
content: Distance between the string and the closest string of the cluster (that is, the minimum distance to any member of the cluster)

label: text
content: Distance between the string and the furthest string of the cluster (that is, the maximum distance to any cluster member)

label: text
content: The average distance between the string and all the strings of the cluster

label: text
content: - More complex methods, considering both the average distance to the cluster members and to other strings outside of the cluster (e.g., "neighbor joining"), have been introduced ...

label: text
content: Distances string - cluster

label: text
content: 3: = average of all distances

label: text
content: ## Measuring distances

label: text
content: - For the distance between two alignments (two clusters) the main choices are:

label: text
content: Distance of the closest pair of members (one from each cluster)

label: text
content: Distance of the farthest pair of members (one from each cluster)

label: text
content: Average distance between all pairs of members (one from each cluster)

label: text
content: - More complex methods, considering both the members of the two clusters and the data points (strings) outside the clusters, have been introduced (e.g., neighbor joining also for this case)

label: text
content: Distances cluster - cluster

label: text
content: 1: = closest pair

label: text
content: 2: = farthest pair

label: text
content: 3: = average of all pairs

label: text
content: ## Measuring distances

label: text
content: Neighbor joining has turned out to be the best choice for multiple sequence alignment

label: text
content: - A variation of the "average" distance principle

label: text
content: - The measure employed is a score that combines

label: text
content: - the distance (average) between the two objects (single sequences and/or alignments) compared, which has to be small, and

label: text
content: - the distance of the two objects from all other objects, which has to be as large as possible

label: text
content: - It is the relationship between these distances which determines which objects to merge in a given step of the algorithm

label: text
content: Essentially, two objects which are very close to each other but also rather close to other objects need not be the best choice

label: text
content: - Two object which are a little farther away from each other but very far from everything else might be the better choice!

label: text
content: - Multiple sequence alignment based on this approach is very fast and considered to produced reliably "good" guide trees

label: text
content: ## "Progressive" multiple alignments

label: text
content: - The approach we have seen has become the de facto standard for solving the MSA problem

label: text
content: Heuristic: since we make a mistake if we insert a gap in the wrong place, we best start with aligning strings where the mistake is less likely!

label: text
content: Thus, if the closest strings are aligned correctly, they can guide the alignment of the more distant strings, which are more likely to be aligned wrongly

label: text
content: No performance guarantee: the procedure does not even take the final SP score into account; so there is no explicit maximization! (But it still turns out to be the approach that works best ...)

label: text
content: ## The local multiple alignment problem

label: text
content: What we have discussed so far is the global version of multiple sequence alignment because we fully aligned all input sequences

label: text
content: The local version of the problem can be formalized as well:

label: text
content: - Find the combination of substrings, one per input string, that produces the multiple alignment with the overall highest score

label: text
content: - With dynamic programming (hypercube...) we can solve it exactly:

label: text
content: - Like for the case of two sequences (matrix), we just need to adjust the way we fill the single cells (including a score of 0 among the possible choices) and then look for the highest score in the entire (hyper)cube!

label: text
content: - Same time/space complexity as the optimal global MSA!

label: text
content: But for a much faster, heuristic method we have an increased difficulty; we have to deal with two problems:

label: text
content: Choose the substrings to be aligned (number of combinations again exponential in $k$)

label: text
content: Multiple alignment of the chosen substrings (that we have just seen is an NP-hard problem)

label: text
content: - As usually done in modern bioinformatics, we formalize the problem in an "easier" way, which is still able to capture the "biological meaning" of the problem

label: text
content: ## Why local multiple alignments?

label: text
content: - A typical scenario/use case for local MSA:

label: text
content: A large set of strings (could be even thousands), no longer than 1,000 characters

label: text
content: - The substrings forming the "biologically optimal" solutions are expected to be much shorter (about 10-15 characters)

label: text
content: - The substrings forming the "biologically optimal" solutions differ only by substitutions (=mismatches), not by insertions/deletions (=gaps)

label: text
content: - Hence, the second step (building the multiple alignment) becomes much easier: what remains to be solved is to find the "best combination" of substrings, that produce the alignment of maximum score

label: text
content: ## Example:

label: text
content: - Thousands of DNA regions (hundreds of nucleotides each) where a protein of interest (e.g., a transcription factor) binds; obtained, e.g., from a ChIP-seq experiment

label: text
content: Goal: determine the DNA sequence pattern (binding site, usually around 5-20 bases) to which the protein binds; the binding sites will be similar to each other but don't need to have precisely the same sequence!

label: text
content: ## Local multiple alignments: formalization

label: text
content: - The most common formalization is even more restrictive:

label: text
content: - Given:

label: text
content: A set of input strings $S_{1}, S_{2}, \dots, S_{k}$

label: text
content: A fixed substring length $w$

label: text
content: A function $f ( x )$ for the evaluation of the multiple alignment

label: text
content: - Problem:

label: text
content: - Find the set of $k$ substrings of length $w$, one per input string, that produces the alignment of maximum score according to function $f(x)$

label: text
content: - This problem is also known as "motif finding": that is, the input strings share a "recurring motif" appearing as substrings within them

label: text
content: - Typical problem of "combinatorial optimization", that is, finding the "optimal object" (the best combination of substrings) among a finite set of objects (all possible combinations of substrings)

label: text
content: - But, even in this "reduced" form the problem remains NP-hard!

label: text
content: Assuming all input strings have length n, there are n-w+1 substrings of length w per string, and thus a total of $( n-w+1 )^{k}$ possible solutions (combination of substrings)!

label: text
content: The problem is exponential in the size of the input ( $k$ strings) ...

label: text
content: - We need heuristic techniques as they are usually employed for solving combinatorial optimization problems

label: text
content: ## Heuristic approach to motif finding

label: text
content: - For motif finding we consider:

label: text
content: For each input string we take exactly one substring

label: text
content: $^{2}$ All substrings which are part of the solution have the same length $k$

label: text
content: There will be no gaps in the final solution

label: text
content: ## Thus:

label: text
content: Any candidate solution can be simply described by a vector of integers $( p_{1}, p_{2}, \dots, p_{k} )$ corresponding to the start positions of the substrings within the k input strings

label: text
content: The final alignment will simply be the respective substrings written one below the other, without gaps

label: text
content: - Hence, for any set of substrings the alignment is well defined and unique

label: text

label: text
content: - In the global MSA, we usually employ the "sum of pairs" score

label: text
content: - It could be used also for the local version of the problem, but it is common practice to use a different function, borrowed from information theory

label: text
content: This measure is not new:

label: text
content: - Known in information theory:

label: text
content: Related to the "Shannon entropy/uncertainty" of set X of events (Shannon, 1948):

label: text
content: The "relative entropy" or "information content" (IC) of the profile, with respect to the "background probabilities" (here: $25 \% = 1 / 4$ ) of the four symbols of the alphabet

label: text
content: - Known in statistics:

label: text
content: The "Kullback-Leibler" divergence (KL divergence) of the observed probability distribution of the symbols (described by the profile) from the "background distribution" of the symbols of the alphabet (Kullback and Leibler, 1951)

label: text
content: - Note: the score can be defined also for "background probabilities" other than 1/4

label: text
content: Some organisms have a "GC-content" different from 50%

label: text
content: Example: the GC-content of Saccharomyces cerevisiae (yeast) is 38%, so the background frequencies would be: 0.19 for G and C, and 0.31 for A and T

label: text
content: ## Motif finding: scoring

label: text
content: - All in all, given

label: text
content: A set of input strings $S_{1}, S_{2}, \dots , S_{k}$ of equal length n

label: text
content: A substring length w

label: text
content: The "information content" score $I C (P)$ for the evaluation of the multiple alignment described as a profile P

label: text
content: - Find the combination of substrings of length w, one per input string, that aligned without gaps produce the profile with maximum IC score

label: text
content: - The "logo" (here: "sequence logo") is a very intuitive way of representing the profile: it is the information content contribution of every symbol in every column (measured in bits for each symbol)

label: formula
text
content: ## Motif finding: exhaustive search

label: text
content: - Align every substring of string $S_{1}$ to every substring of $S_{2}$ — we obtain $O(n^{2})$ profiles

label: text
content: - Align every substring of string $S_{3}$ to every possible $\left( S_{1}, S_{2} \right)$ profile - we obtain $O \left( n^{3} \right)$ profiles

label: text
content: - Align every substring of string $S_{4}$ to every $(S_{1}, S_{2}, S_{3})$ profile - we obtain $O(n^{4})$ profiles

label: text
content: - Align every substring of string $S_{k}$ to every $(S_{1}, S_{2}, S3, \dots, S_{k-1})$ profile - we obtain $O(n^{k})$ profiles

label: text
content: - Determine the profile of maximum IC score

label: text
content: - In this way we generate all possible solutions: we have to find a way to reduce the search space!

label: text
content: ## Possible approach: branch and bound

label: text
content: - Algorithmic approach that reduces the search space by discarding partial solutions in advance if they cannot lead to the optimal solution

label: text
content: But the time complexity remains exponential

label: text
content: ## Motif finding: greedy algorithm

label: text
content: - Align every substring of string $S_{1}$ to every substring of $S_{2}$ - we obtain $O\left(n^{2}\right)$ profiles - keep only the best n profiles according to their IC score

label: text
content: - Align every substring of string $S_{3}$ to the n best $\left( S_{1}, S_{2} \right)$ profiles - we obtain $O\left(n^{2}\right)$ profiles - keep only the best n profiles according to their IC score

label: text
content: - Determine the best profile from the last $O(n^{2})$ profiles

label: text
content: - In this way we do not explore all the solutions, by only a polynomial subset of them

label: text
content: - The algorithm is greedy because at every step (except the last), we keep only what are "locally" the best solutions

label: text
content: If only a subset of the $( S_{1}, S_{2} )$ substring combinations is kept after the first step, there is no longer the guarantee that we will find the optimal solution

label: text
content: - The same holds true for every successive step: there is always the risk of discarding a combination of substrings that would lead to the optimal solution

label: text
content: ## Greedy algorithms

label: text
content: - The same strategy can be designed for a large number of combinatorial problems that can be formalized in a similar way

label: text
content: - In our case, the solution is given by $k$ integer variables $p_{i}$ , telling us the positions (offsets) of the substrings within the strings $S_{i}$ that are included in the solution

label: text
content: - That is, a solution is an assignment of a value to each of the k variables describing the alignment

label: text
content: In general, the greedy approach for problems that can be formalized in this way can me summarized as illustrated in the right column

label: text
content:
- Given k discrete variables

  X1...Xk

label: text
content: - Goal: find the values for the variables that maximize a given function f(X1...Xk)

label: text
content: Find the values of X1, X2 that maximize f(X1,X2): let x1, x2 be these values

label: text
content: 2 Find the value of X3 that maximizes f(X1,X2,X3) with X1=x1, X2=x2 found at the previous step

label: text
content: Find the value of Xk that maximizes

label: text
content: f(X1,X2,...,X(k-1),Xk), given the values x1, x2, ..., x(k-1) found at the previous steps

label: text
content: ## Greedy algorithms

label: text
content: - The algorithm to the right takes at each step only the single best solution found at the previous step

label: text
content: - The number of solutions kept at each step can be extended to more than one (i.e. keep the b best solutions) as long as at each step the number of solutions we have to evaluate remains polynomial in the size of the input

label: text
content: In our problem, we kept $O(n)$ solutions, hence evaluated $O(n^{2})$ solutions at each step

label: text
content: - Advantage of a greedy algorithm: massively reduced time complexity

label: text
content: Disadvantage: can get "stuck" in local optimum; finding the globally best solution is not guaranteed

label: text
content:
- Given k discrete variables

  X1...Xk

label: text
content: - Goal: find the values for the variables that maximize a given function f(X1...Xk)

label: text
content: Find the values of X1, X2 that maximize f(X1,X2): let x1, x2 be these values

label: text
content: 2 Find the value of X3 that maximizes f(X1,X2,X3) with X1=x1, X2=x2 found at the previous step

label: text
content: Find the value of Xk that maximizes

label: text
content: f(X1,X2,...,X(k-1),Xk), given the values x1, x2, ..., x(k-1) found at the previous steps

label: text
content: ## Combinatorial optimization: exploring the search space

label: text
content: - A solution to the problem is an assignment of a value between 1 and $( n-w+1 )$ to k discrete variables $X_{1}, X_{2}\dots X_{k}$ (assuming all strings have length n)

label: text
content: - Hence, each candidate solution to the problem can be seen as a point in a $k$-dimensional "search space" (or "solution space") of the problem

label: text
content: - In our case there are $( n-w+1 )^{k}$ points that can be visited in the search space

label: text
content: - Idea:

label: text
content: - "Explore" the search space, moving from point to point, visiting a polynomial number of points, hoping to visit the one that corresponds to the optimal solution

label: text
content: - The steps in the search space are taken according to a given heuristic

label: text
content: - Nothing is guaranteed for the approximation/solution of the problem: but in practice there are a few "common sense" heuristics that work very well on several problems of this type

label: text
content: ## Exploring the search space: local search

label: text
content: - We start at a point in the k-dimensional space, chosen at random or with some heuristic

label: text
content: - We "look around" at the neighboring points and compute their scores

label: text
content: - We choose the point that will bring the best improvement ("steepest" increase): it will correspond to the new solution

label: text
content: - From this new solution we "look around" and move again ...

label: text
content: - We keep moving like this until we find a point at which no further improvement of the objective function is possible

label: text
content: - This point is a local maximum (hopefully the global maximum)

label: text
content: ## Exploring the search space: local search

label: text
content: We start at "4". After two steps we reach 56

label: text
content: We start at "6". After two steps we reach 58

label: text
content: (Note: in both cases we don't reach the global maximum)

label: text
content: ## Exploring the search space: local search

label: text
content: "Looking around" in the search space at neighboring points corresponds to changing the value of one or more of the variables in the current solution

label: text
content: - One possible way is to select one variable $X_{i}$ keeping the other variables fixed and choose the value $X_{i}$ that brings the best improvement

label: text
content: - If changing $X_{i}$ doesn't improve the solution, we keep the previous value

label: text
content: - We iterate this step, by cycling over the $X_{j}$ variables one by one

label: text
content: This is the equivalent to moving in one direction in the k-dimensional space, going to the "maximum" point we see in that direction

label: text
content: ## Exploring the search space: local search

label: text
content: - This local search technique is sometimes referred to as "hill climbing"

label: text
content: - The local search stops when we find a maximum (or minimum in case we have a minimization problem)

label: text
content: - The "steepest" increase that we choose at given point does not necessarily lead to the global maximum

label: text
content: - We can get "stuck" in a local maximum, and hence find a sub-optimal solution

label: text
content: In this example: from the point P(0), the "steeper increase is in direction of the red arrow; but the global maximum is in direction of the blue arrow

label: text
content: ## Exploring the search space: local search

label: text
content: - The result of the search is clearly dependent on the starting point (the initial "random" solution)

label: text
content: - So, where to start?

label: text
content: - A good choice is to iterate the whole algorithm many times (anyway a polynomial number) with different starting points and to output the best solution found across all searches

label: text
content: In our example, with k sequences of length n, we could run n iterations, which is still fast enough

label: text
content: - The success depends on the "shape" of the optimization function in the k-dimensional space

label: text
content: The more local maxima the lower chances to find the optimal solution

label: text
content: The chance of finding the global maximum (or at least a better local maximum) is increased by starting from different points and reporting the best solution across all searches

label: text
content: ## Implementing a local search

label: text
content: - The rationale is clear, but there are a few implementation details that have to be specified:

label: text
content: How to choose the initial solution (initial alignment as starting point)?

label: text
content: ★ Completely at random or according to some criterion?

label: text
content: How to process the strings (variables)?

label: text
content: ★ In a specific order or in random order?

label: text
content: How to define the neighborhood for the next step?

label: text
content: - Easy for the 2D grid of the example; but for strings?

label: text
content: - Several different choices are possible

label: text
content: ▶ If/when to stop the local search?

label: text
content: How many times to repeat the local search with a different starting point

label: text
content: ## Binary variables:

label: text
content: In the simplest case the $k$ discrete variables $X_{1}, X_{2} \dots X_{k}$ are binary variables

label: text
content: The search space has in this case cardinality $2^{k}$ (number of candidate solutions)

label: text
content: NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems derived from real case applications can often be modeled with binary variables

label: text
content: Example of problems: MAX-CUT, MAX-3-SAT, (0-1) KNAPSACK, etc.

label: text
content: ## MAX-CUT

label: text
content: "Famous" NP-hard problem for combinatorial optimization

label: text
content: - Given a graph $(V, E)$ , find the partition of the vertices/nodes into two subsets $V_{1}, V_{2}$ with $V_{1}\cup V_{2}=V$ such that the number of edges connecting one node of the first partition $V_{1}$ with one node of the second partition $V_{2}$ is maximized

label: text
content: - That is, the two node sets can be separated by "cutting" a maximum number of edges

label: text
content: - Thus, given k vertices, each solution can be described by k binary variables $X_{1}, X_{2} \dots X_{k}$ indicating to which of the two subsets $(V_{1}$ or $V_{2}$ each node belongs (search space of size $2^{k}!$

label: text
content: - $f \left( X_{1}, X_{2} \dots X_{k} \right)$ is the objective function to be optimized

label: text
content: White/black corresponds to the two subsets in which the vertices have been partitioned

label: text
content: ## MAX-CUT

label: text
content: - Initialization: random assignment of each binary variable $X_{i}$ (with probability = 0.5, like a coin toss)

label: text
content: - Variables are updated one by one, from $X_{1}$ to $X_{k}$

label: text
content: - Let $X_{i}=x_{i}$ be the current value of every variable $X_{i}$ - hence we are at point $\left(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{i},\ldots,x_{k}\right)$ of the search space

label: text
content: - The neighborhood is just one additional point: $\left( x_{1}, x_{2}, \dots , \overline{x_{i}}, \dots , x_{k} \right)$ where $\overline{x_{i}}=0$ if $x_{i}=1$ and $\overline{x_{i}}=1$ if $x_{i}=0$ (logical NOT of the current value)

label: text
content: White/black corresponds to the two subsets in which the vertices have been partitioned

label: text
content: - If $f(x_{1}, x_{2}, \dots, \overline{x_{i}}, \dots, x_{k}) > f(x_{1}, x_{2}, \dots, x_{i}, \dots, x_{k})$, then we move to point $(x_{1}, x_{2}, \dots, \overline{x_{i}}, \dots, x_{k})$, which becomes the new current solution

label: text
content: - This is repeated over all the variables $X_{i}$ until a complete cycle over all the variables is completed without any improvement of the solution

label: text
content: ## Local search for the local MSA problem

label: text
content: Problem:

label: text
content: - Input: k strings of length n

label: text
content: - The local alignment is formed of substrings of length $w$

label: text
content: - In this case a solution to the problem is an assignment of values between 1 and $( n-w+1 )$ to $k$ discrete variables $X_{1}, X_{2} \dots X_{k}$

label: text
content: - We start with an initial solution $P (0)$ to the problem, either by choosing one random substring per input sequence, or using some heuristic

label: text
content: Defining the neighborhood:

label: text
content: The usual approach is to select one dimension, to "fix" all other dimensions, and to consider all possible alternatives in the selected dimension as "neighborhood"

label: text
content: - Here: we select one $X_{i}=p_{i}$ (position of the chosen substring within the string i) and try—as neighborhood—all possible values ranging from 1 to $(n-w+1)$

label: text
content: - For our problem this means:

label: text
content: Select an $X_{i}$ (a variable to be updated)

label: text
content: 2 Remove the substring corresponding to $X_{i}$ from the current solution

label: text
content: For each $j \in[1,n-w+1]$ , compute the IC score by setting $X_{i}=j$ (inserting the corresponding substring) and leaving all other variables (substrings) unchanged

label: text
content: Choose $j$ such that $X_{j} = j$ corresponds to the profile with the highest IC score

label: text
content: 5 Adjust the alignment accordingly and select the next $X_{i}$ to update

label: text
content: We remove it from the profile, replacing it with every other substring of S2 and evaluating the profile resulting from each. We replace it with the one yielding the highest IC score

label: text
content: New profile, containing a different string from S2 with higher IC score with respect to the starting one

label: text
content: ## Defining iterations:

label: text
content: In general, we want one "cycle" of steps to update each of the k variables which define a potential solution

label: text
content: - For our problem there are two possible choices:

label: text
content: Process the variables $X_{i}$ in order from 1 to $k$

label: text
content: 2 Process the variables in a random order, using a different random permutation at each cycle

label: text
content: - In practice, there is no big difference in the results for our problem, but for some other problems the "randomized" version is to be preferred

label: text
content: - Using the "random" permutation implies that we might get different results even when starting from the same initial point

label: text
content: - The algorithm will stop at a local maximum in a finite number of steps, where for a full cycle (of all variables) no improvement is obtained

label: text
content: - To be iterated several times with different starting profiles (to increase the chance of finding the global maximum)

label: text
content: ## Improving the local search

label: text
content: Local search is "deterministic", it always chooses the best alternative for improving the current solution

label: text
content: - The major problem of this approach: the existence of (possibly too many) local maxima in which we can get "stuck"

label: text
content: - Can we overcome this problem?

label: text
content: The idea is to make the choice of "non optimal" steps (the one in red) in order to overcome local maxima Whether these steps can be accepted or not it is governed by a random choice

label: text
content: ## Solution: "stochastic optimization"

label: text
content: (not to be confused with "randomized algorithms"!)

label: text
content: - Transform the deterministic algorithm into a stochastic algorithm (stochastic search!)

label: text
content: Take into consideration also sub-optimal alternatives

label: text
content: Given different choices, choose a solution at random but with the probability being influenced by the change in the objective function (e.g., the higher the score increase, the higher the probability to choose the solution)

label: text
content: ## Stochastic search

label: text
content: Example: stochastic search for binary variables

label: text
content: $X_{1}, X_{2} \dots X_{k}$ are binary variables

label: text
content: - At step i, we compare the value $X_{i}$ with the logical NOT of its current value (as with MAX-CUT)

label: text
content: - Compute $\Delta f=f\left(x_{1},x_{2},\dots,\overline{x_{i}},\dots,x_{k}\right)-f\left(x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{i},\dots,x_{k}\right);$ we have two possible results:

label: text
content: The update improves the solution, i.e., $\Delta f > 0$ , then move to the new solution

label: text
content: If not, i.e., $\Delta f\leq0$ , we might anyway choose to move and update the solution

label: text
content: For $\Delta f\leq0$ , accept the change and update the current solution with probability

label: formula
content:
$$
P [ \text {u p d a t e} X _ {i} ] = e ^ {\frac {\Delta f}{T}} \quad \text {w i t h} \Delta f \leq 0
$$

label: text
content: where $T$ is a parameter that allows for "fine tuning" the degree of randomness:

label: text
content: - Larger $T \Rightarrow$ smaller exponent $\Rightarrow$ higher probability to accept the negative change

label: text
content: - Smaller $T \Rightarrow$ higher exponent $\Rightarrow$ lower probability to accept the negative change

label: text
content: $\star$ For $T \rightarrow 0$, the algorithm becomes deterministic ($P[\textit{update } X_{i}]\rightarrow 0)$

label: text
content: ## ▶ That is, the algorithm makes a

label: text
content: That is, the algorithm makes a random choice whose probability is determined by "how bad" the move to the sub-optimal solution is

label: text
content: The bigger the (negative) change $\Delta f < 0$ , the lower the probability of accepting it

label: text
content: ## Stochastic search

label: formula
text
content: We have additional options to alter the behavior of the algorithm, for example:

label: text
content: - The value for $T$ can be dynamically changed during the execution of the algorithm (see, for example, the Wikipedia page for "simulated annealing $^{1}$ and the long list of "related methods" at the end of that page)

label: text
content: We can start with a high value (high randomness) and decrease it at each iteration (ultimately lowering it to zero), thus making the algorithm more and more deterministic (see graph to the right for an example)

label: text
content: - $T$ represents the "temperature": the higher the temperature, the more randomness (in analogy to the kinetic energy of molecules)

label: text
content: - When it cools down (more deterministic), the "movement" due to kinetic energy slows, until it is finally "cold" and the system stops at the nearest local maximum

label: text
content: ## Stochastic search: Gibbs sampling

label: text
content: Let's apply a stochastic search to the local multiple alignment problem:

label: text
content: - We have $k$ variables $X_{1},\dots X_{k}$ defining, as a possible solution, the substrings' starting points in the original input strings

label: text
content: - At step t, we choose to replace the value of variable $X_{i}$

label: text
content: - We evaluate all the possible values (starting positions) $p_{j}$ that the variable can assume

label: text
content: - Local search would always choose the best $p_{j}$ (the one that yields the maximum value of the IC score by inserting the corresponding substring in the profile)

label: text
content: - Here, the situation is more complex than for binary variables, since we will have substrings other than the best $p_{j}$ which ...

label: text
content: either yield some improvement of the IC score, but not as much as the best $p_{j}$

label: text
content: or make the IC score worse (to different extend) with respect to the previous value

label: text
content: - Compute the $IC(p_{i})$ score for each possible $p_{i}$, i.e., each possible substring for $X_{i}$

label: text
content: - Compute $IC(S_{i}) = \sum_{j=1}^{n-w+1} IC(p_{j})$, the total sum of the ICs for all possible substrings for $X_{i}$ — that is, over the whole string $S_{i}$

label: text
content: - We accept a new value for variable $X_{i}$ with a random choice of probability

label: formula
text
content: ## Stochastic search: Gibbs sampling

label: text
content: - We accept a new value for variable $X_{i}$ with a random choice of probability

label: formula
text
content: - This strategy is known as "Gibbs sampling": $^{2}$

label: text
content: First developed in statistics but adapted to the local MSA problem

label: text
content: In this case, the algorithm remains "stochastic" over time (probabilities don't get dynamically flattened as in the case of simulated annealing), so there is no guarantee that it will converge to a local maximum and stop

label: text
content: It will stop if a complete cycle of updates always rejected the update

label: text
content: Or, more commonly, after a fixed number of iterations, reporting the best solution found along the way (not necessarily the last one, which could be worse)
